public_rationale: The August hearing supports Marcus's factual premise for Cruise and Waymo: both had remote human assistance. It does not establish his literal claim about every public-road vehicle. Waymo also distinguished assistance from driving, so the existence of backup does not independently settle the label truly self-driving. No verified counterexample was found, but the universal claim remains unproven.
limitations: The strongest contemporaneous evidence covers the two San Francisco operators.
Assistance availability is different from continuous supervision or remote control.
The March white paper is explanatory context, not August outcome evidence.

our_interpretation: Use the factual definition supplied in the surrounding sentence: every public-road self-driving system had either an onboard safety driver or remote human assistance available.
Having remote assistance available does not necessarily mean continuous human observation, remote steering, or intervention on every trip.
Use August 1–19, 2023, for the ongoing state described in the publication month.
Do not silently restrict every vehicle on public roads to Cruise and Waymo.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous operational documentation or an adequately comprehensive industry assessment establishes one of the two human-support arrangements for all public-road systems.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A verified public-road self-driving system operated without an onboard safety driver and without remote human assistance.

evidence.explanation: Cruise described monitoring and remote help for unforeseen circumstances; Waymo separately described remote assistance while retaining automated driving control. This establishes the human-support arrangement for the two named operators, not for every public-road system.

Waymo expressly distinguished remote assistance from performance of the driving task. This earlier document explains why human backup does not by itself establish that a car is remotely driven or continuously supervised.
